title: File sync and sharing
summary: Chunking, deduplication, metadata sync and conflicts.
prompt: Design a file sync service: a desktop client keeps a folder in sync across a user’s devices, files can be shared with others, and large files sync efficiently over slow connections.

requirements: Functional: upload changes, download changes from other devices, share folders, version history and restore.
Non-functional: small edits to large files upload only what changed; no silent data loss on conflicts; clients sync within seconds when online.
estimation: 100M users × 10 GB average quota usage ≈ 1 EB logical; dedup and compression reduce physical storage substantially.
Metadata: 100M users × 10,000 files × ~500 bytes ≈ 500 TB, so the metadata store must be sharded (by user or namespace).
api: POST /chunks/check {hashes} → which are missing; PUT /chunks/{hash} uploads one.
GET /changes?cursor= → changes since the cursor, with long-polling or a push channel for notifications.
data: Chunks: content-addressed blobs keyed by SHA-256, stored once in object storage.
File versions: (namespace, path, version, chunk list, size, modified_by) in the metadata DB.
A per-namespace change journal with increasing cursors that clients sync from.
design: The client watches the folder, splits changed files into chunks with content-defined chunking, and asks which chunks the server lacks.
It uploads only missing chunks, then commits the new chunk list against the base version it last saw.
Commits append to the journal; a notification service tells other devices to pull changes after their cursor.
deepDives: Content-defined chunking (rolling hash boundaries) keeps most chunks unchanged when bytes are inserted early in a file; fixed-size chunks would all shift.
Conflicts: a commit with a stale base version fails; the client keeps both copies (“conflicted copy”) rather than overwriting.
Dedup across users saves storage but reveals whether a file already exists (an upload that “skips” leaks information); limit dedup to within a user or require proof of possession.
bottlenecks: Large shared folders produce many notifications: batch and coalesce them.
Metadata hot spots for huge namespaces: shard journals and use pagination.
Initial sync of a large account: prioritise recent files, download lazily (placeholders) on demand.
tradeoffs: Smaller chunks = better dedup and smaller re-uploads, but more metadata and requests.
Strong consistency for metadata commits; eventual for the notifications that trigger sync.
Keeping conflicted copies is safe but annoying; automatic merges are only safe for specific file types.

rubric.text: Split files into chunks and uploaded only missing ones.
Separated metadata (versions, journal) from content storage.
Synced via a change journal with cursors and notifications.
Detected conflicts with base versions and never silently overwrote.
Estimated storage and metadata size; sharded metadata.
Explained content-defined chunking and its benefit.
Identified the cross-user dedup privacy leak.
